In the 1950s, Tokyo’s Haneda Airport witnessed an extraordinary event on an ordinary day, revolving around a man who claimed to come from Taured—a country that does not exist on any map or in any history book. A man, dressed indistinguishably from any businessman from anywhere in the world, disembarked from a plane, carrying an elegant briefcase and wearing a suit. When customs officers checked his passport, they paused in confusion. The passport was issued by the Republic of Taured—a country neither heard of nor seen by the officers. The man could not comprehend their bafflement; to him, Taured had been a well-established country located between France and Spain for centuries. He was taken to a room in the airport for further investigation. During the interrogation, the man’s story became even more intriguing. He detailed Taured’s history, culture, and even its political relations with precision. However, the more he elaborated, the more bewildered the authorities became, as Taured did not exist in their world. The man was accommodated in a hotel for the night, with the door locked from the outside and the window too high to permit any escape, making his disappearance impossible. Yet, the next morning, the man inside the room had vanished. The door remained locked, the window untouched, his belongings still in the room, but the man had evaporated into thin air. Over the years, this event spread widely. To some, it is definitive proof of parallel universes; to others, it narrates the tale of a traveler from beyond time. However, the incident of the man from Taured challenges our perception of reality. It reminds us that there might be much more than we know, that the world could be more complex and incomprehensible than it appears.
